02_ask/ask_answers.as_written.question: How is the risk score made?

2026-11-19.summary: Every project gets one risk score from 1 (good) to 4 (bad), made from 70 signals in 16 factors.
2026-11-19.summary_markdown: **Every project gets one risk score from 1 (good) to 4 (bad), made from 70 signals in 16 factors.**
points: Each signal scores 1 to 4 on a written rule. A factor is the weighted average of its signals.
The factors are weighted into two halves, what we control and what we do not, and the project score is the average of the two.
Under 1.5 rates 1, under 2.5 rates 2, under 3.5 rates 3, the rest 4.
Red flags: lawsuits threatened; talk of in-house operation or a re-bid. One of these at its worst rates a project at least 3.
What is at stake (revenue, margin, months left) is read beside the score. It sets which high-risk projects come first.
The scoring is from your template (Contract_Risk_Scorecard_Template.xlsx), used as written. You can change it on the goal's Plan tab.

02_ask/ask_answers.demo_run.question: How is the risk score made?

2026-11-19.summary: Every project gets one risk score from 1 (good) to 4 (bad), made from 70 signals in 16 factors.
2026-11-19.summary_markdown: **Every project gets one risk score from 1 (good) to 4 (bad), made from 70 signals in 16 factors.**
points: Each signal scores 1 to 4 on a written rule. A factor is the weighted average of its signals.
The factors are weighted into two halves, what we control and what we do not, and the project score is the average of the two.
Under 1.5 rates 1, under 2.5 rates 2, under 3.5 rates 3, the rest 4.
Red flags: lawsuits threatened; talk of in-house operation or a re-bid. One of these at its worst rates a project at least 3.
What is at stake (revenue, margin, months left) is read beside the score. It sets which high-risk projects come first.

2026-11-20.summary_markdown: **Every project gets one risk score from 1 (good) to 4 (bad), made from 71 signals in 16 factors.**
points: Each signal scores 1 to 4 on a written rule. A factor is the weighted average of its signals.
The factors are weighted into two halves, what we control and what we do not, and the project score is the average of the two.
Under 1.5 rates 1, under 2.5 rates 2, under 3.5 rates 3, the rest 4.
Red flags: lawsuits threatened; talk of in-house operation or a re-bid; boil water notices in the last twelve months. One of these at its worst rates a project at least 3.
What is at stake (revenue, margin, months left) is read beside the score. It sets which high-risk projects come first.
The scoring is from your template (Contract_Risk_Scorecard_Template.xlsx), used as written. You can change it on the goal's Plan tab.

fromGoal.title: Contract risk: every contract scored, and watched every morning

sections.heading: What this plan is for
sections.body:
One action for every signal at 3 or 4 that can be moved, with an owner, a date and the score it would bring.

Goal: Monitor the risk of every contract in the portfolio on a scorecard built with you: what to measure, how to score it and how much each thing counts. Read every source each morning, and when the risk of a contract goes up say why, with the evidence, and what to do at that site.
Decision asked: What to do about each contract that changed, and who does it
Deadline: The demand letter asks for a response within 30 days, by 19 December

sections.heading: Why the score went up
sections.body:
1. 3 of the 300 contracts changed overnight: Ashby Falls moved from 2 to 3; Harlow Creek moved from 2 to 3; Red Mesa rose from 1.65 to 1.67, still rated 2.
Every reading was read again at 06:00 and scored on your scorecard. Ashby Falls Water and Sewer: talk of in-house operation or a re-bid from 1 to 4, the contract in public meetings from 2 to 3, recent competitor wins from 2 to 4 (a red flag). Harlow Creek WWTP: lawsuits threatened from 2 to 4, odor complaints from 3 to 4 (a red flag). Red Mesa Regional Water Reclamation Facility: required samples missed from 2 to 3. One rating is the average of what we control and what we do not.

3. Red Mesa rose to 1.67 and still rates 2: a second missed sample, with one licence holder covering weekends.
A second missed sample this quarter was recorded on 19 November, so Missed samples goes from 2 to 3 and the internal score from 1.74 to 1.78. On its own that moves nothing. Together with two operator posts open more than 60 days and overtime at 14.2% of payroll it is the combination five of the seven sites with a notice of violation since 2024 showed 8 to 12 weeks before. Both missed samples fell on weekend shifts covered on overtime by the one operator who holds the licence the contract requires.

sections.heading: The plan for each site
sections.body:
Run the full plan at every contract that rose: an odor plan at Harlow Creek, a renewal plan at Ashby Falls, cover at Red Mesa (preferred)
Harlow Creek: an odor source survey, load-out moved to mornings, the complaint calls returned and the Regional VP in front of the City Manager before the 8 December council. Ashby Falls: the Regional VP meets the new DPW Director before 2 December and the renewal plan starts now. Red Mesa: both posts covered from the West float pool on Monday and the sampling schedule given a second owner.
Contracts acted on: 3 of 300 · Revenue they carry: $17.3M a year · Plans written: 3, one per site · Written for: each site, by signal
Trade-off: Three regions get work this week, one of them for a contract that still rates 2.

Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
Contracts acted on: 1 of 300 · Actions opened: 7 · Red Mesa: pattern left to run · Ashby Falls: council meets first
Trade-off: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
Done today: Owners told · Days used of the 30: 13 · Odor survey: not started · Disruption this week: none
Trade-off: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

• Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
• Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Run the full plan at every contract that rose: an odor plan at Harlow Creek, a renewal plan at Ashby Falls, cover at Red Mesa
recs.summary: Harlow Creek: an odor source survey, load-out moved to mornings, the complaint calls returned and the Regional VP in front of the City Manager before the 8 December council. Ashby Falls: the Regional VP meets the new DPW Director before 2 December and the renewal plan starts now. Red Mesa: both posts covered from the West float pool on Monday and the sampling schedule given a second owner.
recs.tradeoff: Three regions get work this week, one of them for a contract that still rates 2.

story.text: The watch fired: three contracts changed overnight. What should be done about each?
Read the demand letter and the complaint log for Harlow Creek.
Read the agreement: liability is capped, consequential damages are not waived, odor capital is the City's.
Harlow Creek crosses from 2 to 3 on your scorecard.
Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
Ashby Falls puts in-house operation on its 2 December agenda, seven months before the contract ends.
Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
recs.summary: Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
recs.tradeoff: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

story.text: What if only a rating change triggers work?
One contract changed rating.
The Ashby Falls board discusses in-house operation on the day of the portfolio review.
Faithful to the scorecard, and late for the two it does not yet see.

recs.title: Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
recs.summary: Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
recs.tradeoff: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

story.text: What if the decisions wait for the leadership team?
The claims procedure asks for Legal within one working day and the insurer within 30.
The review is 12 days away; the letter gives 30.
Allowed by the procedure, costly for the odor plan and for Ashby Falls.

Done. **All 300 projects have one risk score each: 52 rate 3 or 4.** The **contract risk dashboard, version 1**, is published. Open any project for its score, why it scores that, and a mitigation plan written for that site.

**Where you open it, every time:** **Submissions** in the left menu, under “Contract risk dashboard”. It is also on this goal’s **Deliverables** tab, which is open on the right now. Both show the same dashboard.

From now on I read every signal each morning at 06:00 and refresh the dashboard, so what you open is always the latest. The version number changes only when you change the scoring: a signal, a weight or a rule. The next check is tomorrow’s morning check, 06:00 on 20 November. When a score rises I follow your 7 rules: 6 run by themselves, 1 wait for your OK. You can change the scoring at any time on the Plan tab; that is what makes version 2.
Simulate tomorrow’s morning check (20 November)
20 Nov · 06:00 check · 300 contracts · rule fired · 3 changed, 1 moved up a rating

Running the five steps now; then I do what your rules say and tell you.

Step 3 done · what is at stake weighed · Harlow Creek now high risk with a lot at stake
Step 4 done · a mitigation plan written for each site that rose

Top recommendation chosen · option 1

journey.title: Contract risk: every contract scored, and watched every morning
journey.prompt: I need to monitor the risk of all the contracts in our portfolio. Work out what the important risk factors and signals are from everything we have connected, and help me build the scorecard: what to measure, how to score it and how much each thing counts. Then watch every contract, and tell me when the risk of one goes up, why, and what we should do about it at that site.

reads.res: Operations data hub (214 tables), the contract repository (2,460 documents), three shared mailboxes and the public web
300 active operations and maintenance projects in five regions, $1,375.4M a year, booked under 267 profit centers and running 425 facilities. I give each project one score

reads.tool: look for a scoring template you already use
reads.res: None is connected. I found your Contracting Policy (the non-negotiable terms), three loss reviews and the monthly KPI pack, but nothing that says what to score and how. Upload yours, or I propose one

reads.tool: read the contracts you lost or left since 2021
reads.res: 7 contracts: 3 lost at renewal, 2 taken in-house, 2 ended early. What came first in each: a new client lead (5 of 7), margin under budget (7 of 7), in-house operation on a public agenda (both in-house losses)
richstatespoorstates.org (state liability ranking, 2026 edition) · EPA ECHO (permits) · FEMA flood maps · council and board agendas · municipal bond ratings

Not everything is recorded by project. Finance figures are booked by profit center, compliance and maintenance by facility, the client survey by client account. I say how each one is brought to the project and ask you to confirm

questions.title: Do you have a scoring template?
questions.text: A file with your factors and their weights, the signals in each factor, and how each signal scores 1 to 4. If you have one I use it exactly as written. If not, I propose a scorecard. Either way it appears on the right once you answer.

tiles.t: Yes, I will upload it
tiles.s: Use our factors, weights and rules as written

tiles.t: No. Propose one
tiles.s: From what is connected and the contracts already lost

questions.title: This is how every project will be scored
questions.text: The scorecard is on the Plan tab: every factor with its share of the final score, every signal with its weight and its rule for 1 to 4. Drop a signal, add one to a factor, add a factor, or change a weight or a rule, there or here in the chat. The preview shows what each change does to your projects.

tiles.t: Score on it as it stands now
tiles.s: You can change it at any time, also after the goal is live

questions.title: The data check: a few assumptions need your call
questions.text: I tested every signal against the connected data. Most are ready. Some figures do not sit at project level (profit center, facility, client account), and one signal has no source. The data check on the plan lists each signal, how it is measured, and the assumptions I would make to get one figure per project.

tiles.t: Confirm the assumptions as they stand
tiles.s: Or change any of them on the plan first

nodes.title: Read every signal again and re-score
nodes.purpose: Which contracts changed, and by how much.
nodes.how: Every signal of every contract read again from its source and scored on your bands; factor scores from your weights; the contracts whose readings changed, with the old and the new score.
nodes.check: Each score recomputes from its signals, bands and weights.

nodes.title: Read the evidence behind each change
nodes.purpose: Why it changed, and what the contract says about it.
nodes.how: The message, document, row or page behind each changed reading; then the agreement: liability, who pays for the fix, how the client can leave.
nodes.check: Every change points at a dated message, row or page.

nodes.title: Weigh what is at stake and where it is heading
nodes.purpose: Which of the contracts that rose come first.
nodes.how: Annual revenue, margin, months to a decision and how the contract can end, beside the risk; the twelve-month direction of each score; anything I read that your scorecard does not score.
nodes.check: What is at stake never changes the risk score unless you asked for it.

nodes.title: Write the mitigation plan for each site
nodes.purpose: One action for every signal at 3 or 4 that can be moved, for that site.
nodes.how: For each site: the action, written from the reading, the mail about it, the contract clause and what is public; the owner from the contract master, a date, and the score the plan would bring the project to. Facts of the site are listed, not actioned.
draws: The contract master: who owns each contract
nodes.check: Every action names the signal it answers, an owner and a date.

nodes.title: Build the deliverables, act and tell you
nodes.purpose: Build what was agreed at set-up, take the actions that run by themselves, hold the others for your OK, and tell the people you chose.
nodes.how: The dashboard refreshed; then each rule that applies: tell the people named, build the deck on why it moved, write the plan. A rule set to "ask me first" waits for your OK.
draws: Your rules on the Plan tab
nodes.check: Only your rules run. Nothing is sent outside the company.

journey.title: Contract risk: every contract scored, and watched every morning
journey.prompt: I need to monitor the risk of all the contracts in our portfolio. Work out what the important risk factors and signals are from everything we have connected, and help me build the scorecard: what to measure, how to score it and how much each thing counts. Then watch every contract, and tell me when the risk of one goes up, why, and what we should do about it at that site.

reads.res: Operations data hub (214 tables), the contract repository (2,460 documents), three shared mailboxes and the public web
300 active operations and maintenance projects in five regions, $1,375.4M a year, booked under 267 profit centers and running 425 facilities. I give each project one score

reads.tool: look for a scoring template you already use
reads.res: None is connected. I found your Contracting Policy (the non-negotiable terms), three loss reviews and the monthly KPI pack, but nothing that says what to score and how. Upload yours, or I propose one

reads.tool: read the contracts you lost or left since 2021
reads.res: 7 contracts: 3 lost at renewal, 2 taken in-house, 2 ended early. What came first in each: a new client lead (5 of 7), margin under budget (7 of 7), in-house operation on a public agenda (both in-house losses)
richstatespoorstates.org (state liability ranking, 2026 edition) · EPA ECHO (permits) · FEMA flood maps · council and board agendas · municipal bond ratings

Not everything is recorded by project. Finance figures are booked by profit center, compliance and maintenance by facility, the client survey by client account. I say how each one is brought to the project and ask you to confirm

questions.title: Do you have a scoring template?
questions.text: A file with your factors and their weights, the signals in each factor, and how each signal scores 1 to 4. If you have one I use it exactly as written. If not, I propose a scorecard. Either way it appears on the right once you answer.

tiles.t: Yes, I will upload it
tiles.s: Use our factors, weights and rules as written

tiles.t: No. Propose one
tiles.s: From what is connected and the contracts already lost

questions.title: This is how every project will be scored
questions.text: The scorecard is on the Plan tab: every factor with its share of the final score, every signal with its weight and its rule for 1 to 4. Drop a signal, add one to a factor, add a factor, or change a weight or a rule, there or here in the chat. The preview shows what each change does to your projects.

tiles.t: Score on it as it stands now
tiles.s: You can change it at any time, also after the goal is live

questions.title: The data check: a few assumptions need your call
questions.text: I tested every signal against the connected data. Most are ready. Some figures do not sit at project level (profit center, facility, client account), and one signal has no source. The data check on the plan lists each signal, how it is measured, and the assumptions I would make to get one figure per project.

tiles.t: Confirm the assumptions as they stand
tiles.s: Or change any of them on the plan first

nodes.title: Read every signal again and re-score
nodes.purpose: Which contracts changed, and by how much.
nodes.how: Every signal of every contract read again from its source and scored on your bands; factor scores from your weights; the contracts whose readings changed, with the old and the new score.
nodes.check: Each score recomputes from its signals, bands and weights.

nodes.title: Read the evidence behind each change
nodes.purpose: Why it changed, and what the contract says about it.
nodes.how: The message, document, row or page behind each changed reading; then the agreement: liability, who pays for the fix, how the client can leave.
nodes.check: Every change points at a dated message, row or page.

nodes.title: Weigh what is at stake and where it is heading
nodes.purpose: Which of the contracts that rose come first.
nodes.how: Annual revenue, margin, months to a decision and how the contract can end, beside the risk; the twelve-month direction of each score; anything I read that your scorecard does not score.
nodes.check: What is at stake never changes the risk score unless you asked for it.

nodes.title: Write the mitigation plan for each site
nodes.purpose: One action for every signal at 3 or 4 that can be moved, for that site.
nodes.how: For each site: the action, written from the reading, the mail about it, the contract clause and what is public; the owner from the contract master, a date, and the score the plan would bring the project to. Facts of the site are listed, not actioned.
draws: The contract master: who owns each contract
nodes.check: Every action names the signal it answers, an owner and a date.

nodes.title: Build the deliverables, act and tell you
nodes.purpose: Build what was agreed at set-up, take the actions that run by themselves, hold the others for your OK, and tell the people you chose.
nodes.how: The dashboard refreshed; then each rule that applies: tell the people named, build the deck on why it moved, write the plan. A rule set to "ask me first" waits for your OK.
draws: Your rules on the Plan tab
nodes.check: Only your rules run. Nothing is sent outside the company.

recs.title: Run the full plan at every contract that rose: an odor plan at Harlow Creek, a renewal plan at Ashby Falls, cover at Red Mesa
recs.summary: Harlow Creek: an odor source survey, load-out moved to mornings, the complaint calls returned and the Regional VP in front of the City Manager before the 8 December council. Ashby Falls: the Regional VP meets the new DPW Director before 2 December and the renewal plan starts now. Red Mesa: both posts covered from the West float pool on Monday and the sampling schedule given a second owner.
recs.tradeoff: Three regions get work this week, one of them for a contract that still rates 2.

story.text: The watch fired: three contracts changed overnight. What should be done about each?
Read the demand letter and the complaint log for Harlow Creek.
Read the agreement: liability is capped, consequential damages are not waived, odor capital is the City's.
Harlow Creek crosses from 2 to 3 on your scorecard.
Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
Ashby Falls puts in-house operation on its 2 December agenda, seven months before the contract ends.
Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
recs.summary: Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
recs.tradeoff: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

story.text: What if only a rating change triggers work?
One contract changed rating.
The Ashby Falls board discusses in-house operation on the day of the portfolio review.
Faithful to the scorecard, and late for the two it does not yet see.

recs.title: Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
recs.summary: Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
recs.tradeoff: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

story.text: What if the decisions wait for the leadership team?
The claims procedure asks for Legal within one working day and the insurer within 30.
The review is 12 days away; the letter gives 30.
Allowed by the procedure, costly for the odor plan and for Ashby Falls.

journey.title: Contract risk: every contract scored, and watched every morning
journey.prompt: I need to monitor the risk of all the contracts in our portfolio. Work out what the important risk factors and signals are from everything we have connected, and help me build the scorecard: what to measure, how to score it and how much each thing counts. Then watch every contract, and tell me when the risk of one goes up, why, and what we should do about it at that site.

richstatespoorstates.org (state liability ranking, 2026 edition) · EPA ECHO (permits) · FEMA flood maps · council and board agendas · municipal bond ratings

nodes.title: Read every signal again and re-score
nodes.purpose: Which contracts changed, and by how much.
nodes.how: Every signal of every contract read again from its source and scored on your bands; factor scores from your weights; the contracts whose readings changed, with the old and the new score.
nodes.check: Each score recomputes from its signals, bands and weights.

nodes.title: Read the evidence behind each change
nodes.purpose: Why it changed, and what the contract says about it.
nodes.how: The message, document, row or page behind each changed reading; then the agreement: liability, who pays for the fix, how the client can leave.
nodes.check: Every change points at a dated message, row or page.

nodes.title: Weigh what is at stake and where it is heading
nodes.purpose: Which of the contracts that rose come first.
nodes.how: Annual revenue, margin, months to a decision and how the contract can end, beside the risk; the twelve-month direction of each score; anything I read that your scorecard does not score.
nodes.check: What is at stake never changes the risk score unless you asked for it.

nodes.title: Write the mitigation plan for each site
nodes.purpose: One action for every signal at 3 or 4 that can be moved, for that site.
nodes.how: For each site: the action, written from the reading, the mail about it, the contract clause and what is public; the owner from the contract master, a date, and the score the plan would bring the project to. Facts of the site are listed, not actioned.
draws: The contract master: who owns each contract
nodes.check: Every action names the signal it answers, an owner and a date.

nodes.title: Build the deliverables, act and tell you
nodes.purpose: Build what was agreed at set-up, take the actions that run by themselves, hold the others for your OK, and tell the people you chose.
nodes.how: The dashboard refreshed; then each rule that applies: tell the people named, build the deck on why it moved, write the plan. A rule set to "ask me first" waits for your OK.
draws: Your rules on the Plan tab
nodes.check: Only your rules run. Nothing is sent outside the company.

w4.text: Done · a plan for each site

recs.title: Run the full plan at every contract that rose: an odor plan at Harlow Creek, a renewal plan at Ashby Falls, cover at Red Mesa
recs.summary: Harlow Creek: an odor source survey, load-out moved to mornings, the complaint calls returned and the Regional VP in front of the City Manager before the 8 December council. Ashby Falls: the Regional VP meets the new DPW Director before 2 December and the renewal plan starts now. Red Mesa: both posts covered from the West float pool on Monday and the sampling schedule given a second owner.
recs.tradeoff: Three regions get work this week, one of them for a contract that still rates 2.

story.text: The watch fired: three contracts changed overnight. What should be done about each?
Read the demand letter and the complaint log for Harlow Creek.
Read the agreement: liability is capped, consequential damages are not waived, odor capital is the City's.
Harlow Creek crosses from 2 to 3 on your scorecard.
Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
Ashby Falls puts in-house operation on its 2 December agenda, seven months before the contract ends.
Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
recs.summary: Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
recs.tradeoff: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

story.text: What if only a rating change triggers work?
One contract changed rating.
The Ashby Falls board discusses in-house operation on the day of the portfolio review.
Faithful to the scorecard, and late for the two it does not yet see.

recs.title: Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
recs.summary: Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
recs.tradeoff: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

story.text: What if the decisions wait for the leadership team?
The claims procedure asks for Legal within one working day and the insurer within 30.
The review is 12 days away; the letter gives 30.
Allowed by the procedure, costly for the odor plan and for Ashby Falls.

story.text: The watch fired: three contracts changed overnight. What should be done about each?
Read the demand letter and the complaint log for Harlow Creek.

Harlow Creek crosses from 2 to 3 on your scorecard.
Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
Ashby Falls puts in-house operation on its 2 December agenda, seven months before the contract ends.
Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
recs.summary: Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
recs.tradeoff: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

story.text: What if only a rating change triggers work?
One contract changed rating.
The Ashby Falls board discusses in-house operation on the day of the portfolio review.
Faithful to the scorecard, and late for the two it does not yet see.

recs.title: Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
recs.summary: Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
recs.tradeoff: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

story.text: What if the decisions wait for the leadership team?
The claims procedure asks for Legal within one working day and the insurer within 30.
The review is 12 days away; the letter gives 30.
Allowed by the procedure, costly for the odor plan and for Ashby Falls.

story.text: The watch fired: three contracts changed overnight. What should be done about each?
Read the demand letter and the complaint log for Harlow Creek.

Harlow Creek crosses from 2 to 3 on your scorecard.
Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
Ashby Falls puts in-house operation on its 2 December agenda, seven months before the contract ends.
Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
recs.summary: Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
recs.tradeoff: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

story.text: What if only a rating change triggers work?
One contract changed rating.
The Ashby Falls board discusses in-house operation on the day of the portfolio review.
Faithful to the scorecard, and late for the two it does not yet see.

recs.title: Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
recs.summary: Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
recs.tradeoff: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

story.text: What if the decisions wait for the leadership team?
The claims procedure asks for Legal within one working day and the insurer within 30.
The review is 12 days away; the letter gives 30.
Allowed by the procedure, costly for the odor plan and for Ashby Falls.

story.text: The watch fired: three contracts changed overnight. What should be done about each?
Read the demand letter and the complaint log for Harlow Creek.
Read the agreement: liability is capped, consequential damages are not waived, odor capital is the City's.
Harlow Creek crosses from 2 to 3 on your scorecard.
Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
Ashby Falls puts in-house operation on its 2 December agenda, seven months before the contract ends.
Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
recs.summary: Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
recs.tradeoff: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

story.text: What if only a rating change triggers work?
One contract changed rating.
The Ashby Falls board discusses in-house operation on the day of the portfolio review.
Faithful to the scorecard, and late for the two it does not yet see.

recs.title: Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
recs.summary: Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
recs.tradeoff: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

story.text: What if the decisions wait for the leadership team?
The claims procedure asks for Legal within one working day and the insurer within 30.
The review is 12 days away; the letter gives 30.
Allowed by the procedure, costly for the odor plan and for Ashby Falls.

recs.title: Run the full plan at every contract that rose: an odor plan at Harlow Creek, a renewal plan at Ashby Falls, cover at Red Mesa
recs.summary: Harlow Creek: an odor source survey, load-out moved to mornings, the complaint calls returned and the Regional VP in front of the City Manager before the 8 December council. Ashby Falls: the Regional VP meets the new DPW Director before 2 December and the renewal plan starts now. Red Mesa: both posts covered from the West float pool on Monday and the sampling schedule given a second owner.
recs.tradeoff: Three regions get work this week, one of them for a contract that still rates 2.

story.text: The watch fired: three contracts changed overnight. What should be done about each?
Read the demand letter and the complaint log for Harlow Creek.
Read the agreement: liability is capped, consequential damages are not waived, odor capital is the City's.
Harlow Creek crosses from 2 to 3 on your scorecard.
Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
Ashby Falls puts in-house operation on its 2 December agenda, seven months before the contract ends.
Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
recs.summary: Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
recs.tradeoff: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

story.text: What if only a rating change triggers work?
One contract changed rating.
The Ashby Falls board discusses in-house operation on the day of the portfolio review.
Faithful to the scorecard, and late for the two it does not yet see.

recs.title: Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
recs.summary: Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
recs.tradeoff: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

story.text: What if the decisions wait for the leadership team?
The claims procedure asks for Legal within one working day and the insurer within 30.
The review is 12 days away; the letter gives 30.
Allowed by the procedure, costly for the odor plan and for Ashby Falls.

sections.heading: What changed since the last check
sections.body:
1. Overnight, 3 of the 300 contracts changed and one moved a rating: Harlow Creek WWTP in Georgia, from 2 to 3.
All 11,973 readings were read again at 06:00. Four changed, on three contracts. Harlow Creek was the contract closest to the line: its internal score went from 2.35 to 2.40 and its external score from 2.30 to 2.38, so it now rates 3, medium to high. Red Mesa in Arizona and Ashby Falls in Massachusetts changed without moving a rating. The other 297 contracts stand where they stood.

sections.heading: Ratings by region
sections.body:
1. Overnight, 3 of the 300 contracts changed and one moved a rating: Harlow Creek WWTP in Georgia, from 2 to 3.
All 11,973 readings were read again at 06:00. Four changed, on three contracts. Harlow Creek was the contract closest to the line: its internal score went from 2.35 to 2.40 and its external score from 2.30 to 2.38, so it now rates 3, medium to high. Red Mesa in Arizona and Ashby Falls in Massachusetts changed without moving a rating. The other 297 contracts stand where they stood.

2. Harlow Creek: a demand letter for 23 residents arrived at 16:42 and a sixth odor complaint was logged the same evening.
Threatened litigation goes from 2 to 4 (a demand letter is the top band) and Odor complaints from 3 to 4 (more than five in a year). The letter asks for abatement, the odor records since January 2024 and talks on compensation within 30 days, and names the City too. Five of the six complaints fall on biosolids load-out afternoons and two were never called back. The setting makes it worse: Georgia rates 4 on the state ranking (rank 46 of 50) and 11,420 homes sit within 2 miles. The contract caps liability at the annual fee but has no waiver of consequential damages.

3. Red Mesa still rates 2, but it now shows the pattern that came before five of the last seven notices of violation.
A second missed sample this quarter was recorded on 19 November, so Missed samples goes from 2 to 3 and the internal score from 1.74 to 1.78. On its own that moves nothing. Together with two operator posts open more than 60 days and overtime at 14.2% of payroll it is the combination five of the seven sites with a notice of violation since 2024 showed 8 to 12 weeks before. Both missed samples fell on weekend shifts covered on overtime by the one operator who holds the licence the contract requires.

4. Ashby Falls does not move on the scorecard, and it is the contract most likely to be lost: $7.4M a year, ending in seven months.
The Select Board agenda posted on 19 November lists "Water and sewer operations after June 2027: options including in-house operation" for 2 December, with a vote to hire a procurement adviser. The DPW Director changed in August; the NPS of 8 on file was given by her predecessor. The agreement ends 30 June 2027 with no renewal option left, and a competitor presented to the Finance Committee in October. None of this is a signal on the scorecard, so the rating stays 2. It is the same sequence as Calder Valley in 2025.

04_submissions/submissions_after_morning.audience: Renee Halvorsen, SVP, Contract Operations, and the five Regional VPs

fromGoal.title: Contract risk: every contract scored, and watched every morning

sections.heading: Where the portfolio stands
sections.body:
Run the full plan at every contract that rose: an odor plan at Harlow Creek, a renewal plan at Ashby Falls, cover at Red Mesa.
Harlow Creek: an odor source survey, load-out moved to mornings, the complaint calls returned and the Regional VP in front of the City Manager before the 8 December council. Ashby Falls: the Regional VP meets the new DPW Director before 2 December and the renewal plan starts now. Red Mesa: both posts covered from the West float pool on Monday and the sampling schedule given a second owner.
Contracts acted on: 3 of 300
Revenue they carry: $17.3M a year
Plans written: 3, one per site
Written for: each site, by signal

sections.heading: What changed since the last check
sections.body:
1. 3 of the 300 contracts changed overnight: Ashby Falls moved from 2 to 3; Harlow Creek moved from 2 to 3; Red Mesa rose from 1.65 to 1.67, still rated 2.
Every reading was read again at 06:00 and scored on your scorecard. Ashby Falls Water and Sewer: talk of in-house operation or a re-bid from 1 to 4, the contract in public meetings from 2 to 3, recent competitor wins from 2 to 4 (a red flag). Harlow Creek WWTP: lawsuits threatened from 2 to 4, odor complaints from 3 to 4 (a red flag). Red Mesa Regional Water Reclamation Facility: required samples missed from 2 to 3. One rating is the average of what we control and what we do not.

sections.heading: Ratings by region
sections.body:
1. 3 of the 300 contracts changed overnight: Ashby Falls moved from 2 to 3; Harlow Creek moved from 2 to 3; Red Mesa rose from 1.65 to 1.67, still rated 2.
Every reading was read again at 06:00 and scored on your scorecard. Ashby Falls Water and Sewer: talk of in-house operation or a re-bid from 1 to 4, the contract in public meetings from 2 to 3, recent competitor wins from 2 to 4 (a red flag). Harlow Creek WWTP: lawsuits threatened from 2 to 4, odor complaints from 3 to 4 (a red flag). Red Mesa Regional Water Reclamation Facility: required samples missed from 2 to 3. One rating is the average of what we control and what we do not.

2. Harlow Creek: a demand letter for 23 residents arrived at 16:42 and a sixth odor complaint was logged the same evening.
Threatened litigation goes from 2 to 4 (a demand letter is the top band) and Odor complaints from 3 to 4 (more than five in a year). The letter asks for abatement, the odor records since January 2024 and talks on compensation within 30 days, and names the City too. Five of the six complaints fall on biosolids load-out afternoons and two were never called back. The setting makes it worse: Georgia rates 4 on the state ranking (rank 46 of 50) and 11,420 homes sit within 2 miles. The contract caps liability at the annual fee but has no waiver of consequential damages.

3. Red Mesa rose to 1.67 and still rates 2: a second missed sample, with one licence holder covering weekends.
A second missed sample this quarter was recorded on 19 November, so Missed samples goes from 2 to 3 and the internal score from 1.74 to 1.78. On its own that moves nothing. Together with two operator posts open more than 60 days and overtime at 14.2% of payroll it is the combination five of the seven sites with a notice of violation since 2024 showed 8 to 12 weeks before. Both missed samples fell on weekend shifts covered on overtime by the one operator who holds the licence the contract requires.

4. Ashby Falls moves to 3: in-house operation is on the 2 December agenda, seven months before a $7.4M contract ends.
The Select Board agenda posted on 19 November lists "Water and sewer operations after June 2027: options including in-house operation" for 2 December, with a vote to hire a procurement adviser. The DPW Director changed in August; the NPS of 8 on file was given by her predecessor. The agreement ends 30 June 2027 with no renewal option left, and a competitor presented to the Finance Committee in October. None of this is a signal on the scorecard, so the rating stays 2. It is the same sequence as Calder Valley in 2025.

pages:
OPERATIONS AND MAINTENANCE AGREEMENT
City of Harlow Creek, Georgia and Northline Contract Operations, Inc.

2.1 Term. Ten years from 1 July 2018 to 30 June 2028.

3.1 Scope of services. The Operator shall operate and maintain (a) the Harlow Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant, (b) the wastewater collection system including 14 lift stations, and (c) biosolids handling, hauling and disposal.

9.4 Capital improvements. Capital repairs and replacements above $25,000 per item, including odor control equipment and media, are the responsibility of the City. The Operator shall recommend such improvements in the annual capital plan.

9.6 Odor. The Operator shall operate the odor control systems as installed and respond to each odor complaint within one business day.

14.1 Limitation of liability. The Operator's total liability under this Agreement in any contract year shall not exceed the annual fee for that year.

14.2 [Reserved.]

15.1 Indemnification. The Operator shall indemnify the City against third party claims to the extent caused by the negligence or wilful misconduct of the Operator.

Analyst note: 14.1 is a liability cap and 15.1 limits indemnity to negligence. There is no waiver of consequential, special or punitive damages anywhere in the Agreement or its three amendments. One of the three core terms is missing: rating 3, for Legal to confirm.

16.3 Claims. Where a third party claim names both parties, the parties shall cooperate in the defense and may agree a joint defense.

21.1 Termination for convenience. The City may terminate this Agreement on 180 days' written notice.
05_sources_and_catalog/documents.evidence_for: Non-negotiable terms read (liability cap, consequential damages, indemnity), the scope of services, who funds odor control, and how the City can end it.

pages:
CALDER VALLEY WWTP: REVIEW OF THE LOST RENEWAL
Prepared for the Contract Operations leadership team, March 2026

We operated Calder Valley for eleven years without a notice of violation. The County re-bid the contract in 2025 and awarded it to Clearbrook Operations in December. Our price was 4% above theirs.

What changed in the year before:
  March 2025    The utilities director who signed both renewals retired.
  May 2025      The County hired a procurement adviser to "test the market".
  March 2025    The NPS survey went to the retired director's address; no answer was recorded and the last score (9) stayed on file.
  September 2025 Clearbrook presented to the County Commission.
What we would do differently: meet a new client lead within 30 days; treat a score given by a predecessor as no score; read the commission agendas. Plant performance was never the issue.

07_scorecard/design_as_written.what: The scorecard as written: the template as uploaded. The scorecard the analyst proposes gives the same scores. Nothing changed.

07_scorecard/design_demo_run.what: The demo run: the scorecard as written, with the thresholds of "Safety observations per employee" taken from history (3.5, 1.5, 0.5 a year).

07_scorecard/design_version_2.what: Version 2: the demo run scorecard with the two changes asked for in the chat on 20 November. A new signal, Boil water notices in the last twelve months, as a red flag; Days sales outstanding scores 4 from 75 days.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Non-negotiable Contract Terms
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: Contract terms the company should never accept, such as uncapped liability.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Commercial Terms
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: Terms and conditions that make the contract harder or costlier to run.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Permit Compliance
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: Whether the plant meets its permits. Three-year average.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Workforce
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: Whether the site has enough qualified people.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Client Satisfaction
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: How the client feels about us.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Community Standing
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: How residents and local media see the operation.

07_scorecard/factors.name: State Legal Climate
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: How costly the state is for lawsuits.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Asset Condition and Complexity
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: The condition and complexity of the assets we run.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Neighbors
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: How many homes sit near the plant.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Water Quality and Contaminants
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: The water coming in, and the contaminants new rules target.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Financial Performance
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: How the contract is doing commercially. Money problems tend to show before the others.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Client and Political Environment
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: The people and the politics on the client side, where most renewals are decided.

07_scorecard/factors.name: Climate and Operational Resilience
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: Sudden events that no monthly figure predicts.

07_scorecard/factors.name: What is at stake
07_scorecard/factors.what_it_is: How much a loss would matter and how soon. Kept beside the risk score, not inside it.

07_scorecard/history_check.about: For every signal scored on a figure: how the 300 projects are spread, the thresholds as written, and the thresholds history would give (better half scores 1, next 30% score 2, next 15% score 3, worst 5% score 4). Flagged = the written rule puts 60% or more of the projects in one score. Rules that follow a regulatory limit are never flagged.

signals.name: Client survey score for the site
Maintenance hours logged to work orders

07_scorecard/scoring_rules.signal: Each signal scores 1 to 4 on its written rule.
07_scorecard/scoring_rules.factor: A factor is the weighted average of its signals.
07_scorecard/scoring_rules.project: Factors are weighted into two halves (what we control, what we do not control). The project score is the average of the two halves; the person can choose the higher of the two instead.

red_flags.rule: A red-flag signal at its worst case rates the project at least 3 (score floor 2.5).

07_scorecard/scoring_rules.stake: What is at stake is read beside the score and sets the priority; it is not averaged in.

priority.Act now: High risk and a lot at stake
priority.Watch: A lot at stake and close to the line

07_scorecard/scoring_rules.direction: Rose or fell = the score moved by more than 0.08 in 90 days.
07_scorecard/scoring_rules.version_rule: The dashboard gets a new version only when the scoring changes. A morning check refreshes the same version.
